Even now, when he is mixing himself a drink at his private bar in Nuova Volsinii, Demetri still finds himself thinking now and then of that night—the last time he sat down to dinner with everyone at the Bellone house.
That day he had just come from meeting the informant he had planted inside Famiglia Rossetti. When he got home, the antipasti were already laid out on the table. It was no special occasion, and yet it was a rare one: Leon was back from the Construction Department, and Bernardo and Lavinia were there as well. At some point he could not name, the times they all gathered like this around the table had grown fewer and fewer.
He sat down in the place laid with his own cutlery and began, as a matter of course, to speak of what he had learned. But Bernardo glanced at Lavinia, whose face had darkened, and cut him off. He knew that Lavinia was unlike the other judges who had a famiglia behind them, that she held rather different ideas about the 'famiglie' of Siracusa. At the time, though, he assumed that sooner or later she too would become one of the Bellones, and that Bernardo simply judged the moment not yet right—so there were certain things not fit to be said in front of her.
He decided he would report to Bernardo privately later on. In those days the orders Bernardo handed him directly had grown fewer and fewer; more often, Bernardo let him act at his own discretion, and so all of this intelligence he had gathered on his own initiative. As construction of the new mobile city neared completion, every famiglia was stirring, and he judged it necessary to keep a grasp on the movements of the others. That was the duty a strategist of the Bellones ought to shoulder. He would prove to Bernardo that he was a strategist worthy of the name, one to whom the famiglia's future could be entrusted.
Once the stew and the soup had been brought out, he drew the dagger he always carried to cut the meat for everyone at the table and to portion out the soup. By then the heavy air left behind by the Rossettis' movements had lifted. Leon talked animatedly of what he had seen and heard at the Construction Department; Lavinia offered the occasional remark; and Bernardo, though he said little, nodded now and then in agreement. The Construction Department was a place many famiglie had their eyes on, and those sights and stories were laced with the same blood and violence that famiglia feuds have always brought to Siracusa. Yet somehow, coming out of Leon's mouth, they carried a certain hope and vigor, as though the future held changes altogether new, nothing at all like what had come before.
To Demetri at that time, there was a certain naivety running through everything Leon said. But there was nothing wrong with that. A future don ought, of course, to come into contact with all manner of people and affairs, so that when he inherited the Bellones he could survey the whole board better and give the clearest, most decisive instructions—and so that he could better understand and care for every member of the famiglia, and let the Bellones go on growing greater still. Even if the path Leon walked now strayed somewhat from what he had envisioned, Demetri believed that under his own guidance and tutelage, Leon would one day become the most perfect leader the famiglia could have; and when that day came, he himself would be, like the dagger in his hand, Leon's most practical tool.
Thinking back on it now, the only one who was truly naive that night was, in all likelihood, himself.
Demetri carves the ice into a sphere with his dagger and drops it into the glass before him. This dagger has followed him for many years and is practical still. And so is he.
